name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_AR_Q01 - Expanded octet in phosphorus pentachloride and sulphur hexafluoride

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): \(\mathrm{PCl}_{5}\) and \(\mathrm{SF}_{6}\) do not obey the octet rule.

Reason (R): Elements in and beyond the third period of the periodic table have \(d\) orbitals available for bonding in addition to \(s\) and \(p\) orbitals, allowing more than eight valence electrons around the central atom.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the octet rule, atoms combine to attain eight electrons in their valence shell. However, elements in and beyond the third period possess \(3d\) orbitals alongside \(3s\) and \(3p\) orbitals, which have comparable energies and can participate in bonding to form an expanded octet.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
In \(\mathrm{PCl}_{5}\), the central phosphorus atom is surrounded by \(10\) valence electrons (\(5\) bond pairs). In \(\mathrm{SF}_{6}\), the central sulphur atom is surrounded by \(12\) valence electrons (\(6\) bond pairs). Since both central atoms have more than eight electrons, these molecules are exceptions to the octet rule. Thus, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Both phosphorus and sulphur belong to the third period of the periodic table and have vacant \(3d\) orbitals available for bonding in addition to \(3s\) and \(3p\) orbitals, which enables them to accommodate more than eight electrons in their valence shell. Thus, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The availability of \(d\) orbitals in third-period elements directly explains why \(\mathrm{PCl}_{5}\) and \(\mathrm{SF}_{6}\) exhibit an expanded octet and do not obey the octet rule. Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_AR_Q02 - Intramolecular hydrogen bonding in ortho-nitrophenol

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): o-Nitrophenol exhibits intramolecular hydrogen bonding.

Reason (R): The magnitude of hydrogen bonding is maximum in the solid state and minimum in the gaseous state.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An intramolecular hydrogen bond is formed when a hydrogen atom lies between two highly electronegative atoms (\(\mathrm{F}\), \(\mathrm{O}\), or \(\mathrm{N}\)) present within the same molecule. Separately, the extent of hydrogen bonding in a substance depends on its physical state.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
In o-nitrophenol, the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group and the \(-\mathrm{NO}_{2}\) group are adjacent to each other on the benzene ring. This allows the hydrogen atom of the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group to form a hydrogen bond with an oxygen atom of the \(-\mathrm{NO}_{2}\) group within the same molecule. Thus, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
In the solid state, molecules are closely packed and orderly arranged, so hydrogen bonding is maximum; in the gaseous state, molecules are far apart, so hydrogen bonding is minimum. Thus, the Reason is also correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
While both statements are factually true, the dependence of hydrogen bonding magnitude on physical state does not explain why o-nitrophenol forms an intramolecular hydrogen bond. Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_AR_Q03 - Dipole moment comparison between ammonia and nitrogen trifluoride

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): The resultant dipole moment of \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) (\(4.90 \times 10^{-30}\ \mathrm{C\ m}\)) is greater than that of \(\mathrm{NF}_{3}\) (\(0.80 \times 10^{-30}\ \mathrm{C\ m}\)).

Reason (R): In \(\mathrm{NF}_{3}\), the orbital dipole due to the lone pair on nitrogen is in the same direction as the resultant dipole moment of the three \(\mathrm{N-F}\) bonds.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In polyatomic molecules with a lone pair on the central atom, the net dipole moment is the vector sum of the individual bond dipoles and the orbital dipole due to the lone pair.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Both \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) and \(\mathrm{NF}_{3}\) have a trigonal pyramidal shape with one lone pair on nitrogen. Experimentally, the net dipole moment of \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) is \(1.47\ \mathrm{D}\) (\(4.90 \times 10^{-30}\ \mathrm{C\ m}\)), which is much larger than that of \(\mathrm{NF}_{3}\) at \(0.23\ \mathrm{D}\) (\(0.80 \times 10^{-30}\ \mathrm{C\ m}\)). Thus, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
In \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\), nitrogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the \(\mathrm{N-H}\) bond dipoles point toward nitrogen, reinforcing the orbital dipole of the lone pair. In \(\mathrm{NF}_{3}\), fluorine is more electronegative than nitrogen, so the three \(\mathrm{N-F}\) bond dipoles point away from nitrogen toward the fluorine atoms, which is opposite to the direction of the lone pair orbital dipole. Thus, the Reason is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Because the lone pair orbital dipole opposes the resultant of the \(\mathrm{N-F}\) bond dipoles in \(\mathrm{NF}_{3}\) rather than reinforcing it, the Assertion is correct and the Reason is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_AR_Q04 - Bond angle distortion in water and ammonia

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): The \(\mathrm{H-O-H}\) bond angle in \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) (\(104.5^{\circ}\)) is smaller than the \(\mathrm{H-N-H}\) bond angle in \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) (\(107^{\circ}\)).

Reason (R): According to VSEPR theory, the repulsive interaction between electron pairs decreases in the order: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In VSEPR theory, lone pairs are localized on the central atom and occupy more space than bonding pairs, which are shared between two nuclei. Consequently, electron-pair repulsions follow the order: \(\mathrm{lp-lp} > \mathrm{lp-bp} > \mathrm{bp-bp}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Both \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) have four electron pairs around the central atom (tetrahedral electron-pair arrangement with an ideal angle of \(109.5^{\circ}\)). However, \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) has one lone pair and three bond pairs, reducing its bond angle to \(107^{\circ}\), whereas \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) has two lone pairs and two bond pairs, reducing its bond angle further to \(104.5^{\circ}\). Thus, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
The stated order of repulsive interactions (\(\mathrm{lp-lp} > \mathrm{lp-bp} > \mathrm{bp-bp}\)) is a fundamental postulate of VSEPR theory. Thus, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Because \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) has two lone pairs, the strong \(\mathrm{lp-lp}\) repulsion pushes the lone pairs further apart and compresses the \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond pairs more strongly than the single lone pair compresses the \(\mathrm{N-H}\) bond pairs in \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\). Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_AR_Q05 - Axial and equatorial bond lengths in phosphorus pentachloride

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): In \(\mathrm{PCl}_{5}\), the two axial \(\mathrm{P-Cl}\) bonds are slightly longer and weaker than the three equatorial \(\mathrm{P-Cl}\) bonds.

Reason (R): The axial bond pairs in the trigonal bipyramidal geometry of \(\mathrm{PCl}_{5}\) suffer greater repulsive interaction from the equatorial bond pairs.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In \(\mathrm{PCl}_{5}\), the central phosphorus atom undergoes \(sp^{3}d\) hybridisation to form five \(sp^{3}d\) hybrid orbitals directed toward the corners of a trigonal bipyramid.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
In a trigonal bipyramidal molecule, all bond angles are not equivalent. The three equatorial \(\mathrm{P-Cl}\) bonds lie in one plane at \(120^{\circ}\) to each other, while the two axial \(\mathrm{P-Cl}\) bonds lie above and below this plane at \(90^{\circ}\) to the equatorial bonds. Experimentally, the axial bonds are slightly longer and weaker than the equatorial bonds, making \(\mathrm{PCl}_{5}\) reactive. Thus, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Each axial bond pair is at \(90^{\circ}\) to three equatorial bond pairs, whereas each equatorial bond pair is at \(90^{\circ}\) to only two axial bond pairs (and at \(120^{\circ}\) to the other two equatorial bond pairs). Hence, axial bond pairs experience greater repulsion from equatorial bond pairs. Thus, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The greater repulsive interaction experienced by the axial bond pairs causes them to lengthen slightly and become weaker than the equatorial bonds. Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_AR_Q06 - Stability of beryllium molecule and molecular orbital energy order

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): The \(\mathrm{Be}_{2}\) molecule is stable and exists with a bond order of \(1\).

Reason (R): For homonuclear diatomic molecules such as \(\mathrm{B}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\), and \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\), the energy of the \(\sigma 2p_{z}\) molecular orbital is higher than that of the \(\pi 2p_{x}\) and \(\pi 2p_{y}\) molecular orbitals.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to molecular orbital theory, bond order is given by \(\frac{1}{2}(N_{b} - N_{a})\), where \(N_{b}\) is the number of electrons in bonding molecular orbitals and \(N_{a}\) is the number of electrons in antibonding molecular orbitals. A molecule is unstable and does not exist if its bond order is zero or negative.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Each beryllium atom has \(4\) electrons (\(1s^{2} 2s^{2}\)), so \(\mathrm{Be}_{2}\) has \(8\) electrons. Its molecular orbital electronic configuration is \((\sigma 1s)^{2}(\sigma^{*} 1s)^{2}(\sigma 2s)^{2}(\sigma^{*} 2s)^{2}\). Here \(N_{b} = 4\) and \(N_{a} = 4\), giving a bond order of \(\frac{1}{2}(4 - 4) = 0\). Therefore, \(\mathrm{Be}_{2}\) is unstable and does not exist. Thus, the Assertion is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Experimentally, for second-row homonuclear diatomic molecules up to \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\) (such as \(\mathrm{Li}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{Be}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{B}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\), and \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\)), the increasing order of molecular orbital energies places \((\pi 2p_{x} = \pi 2p_{y})\) lower in energy than \(\sigma 2p_{z}\). Thus, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The Assertion is incorrect because \(\mathrm{Be}_{2}\) has zero bond order and does not exist, whereas the Reason correctly states the energy ordering of \(\sigma 2p_{z}\) and \(\pi 2p\) molecular orbitals for \(\mathrm{B}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\), and \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_AR_Q07 - Resonance hybrid nature of the carbonate ion

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): All carbon–oxygen bonds in the carbonate ion (\(\mathrm{CO}_{3}^{2-}\)) are experimentally found to be equivalent.

Reason (R): The carbonate ion exists in a dynamic equilibrium among its three canonical forms, spending equal fractions of time in each form.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Resonance is used when a single Lewis structure cannot accurately represent a molecule or polyatomic ion. In such cases, the actual structure is a resonance hybrid of multiple canonical (contributing) structures.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
A single Lewis structure of \(\mathrm{CO}_{3}^{2-}\) shows two \(\mathrm{C-O}\) single bonds and one \(\mathrm{C=O}\) double bond, which would imply unequal bond lengths. However, experimental measurements confirm that all three carbon–oxygen bonds in \(\mathrm{CO}_{3}^{2-}\) are equivalent. Thus, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Canonical forms have no real existence. A molecule or ion does not spend fractions of time in different canonical forms, nor is there any equilibrium between them (unlike tautomers). Instead, \(\mathrm{CO}_{3}^{2-}\) has a single actual structure, which is the resonance hybrid of the three canonical forms. Thus, the Reason is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Since the equivalence of carbon–oxygen bonds in \(\mathrm{CO}_{3}^{2-}\) arises from a single resonance hybrid structure rather than a dynamic equilibrium among canonical forms, the Assertion is correct and the Reason is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_AR_Q08 - Energetic stability of crystalline sodium chloride

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Solid \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) is stable even though the sum of the ionization enthalpy of \(\mathrm{Na(g)}\) and the electron gain enthalpy of \(\mathrm{Cl(g)}\) is positive.

Reason (R): The energy released during the formation of the crystal lattice of \(\mathrm{NaCl(s)}\) more than compensates for the net energy absorbed during the formation of gaseous \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ions.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The stability of an ionic solid depends not only on the energetics of ion formation in the gaseous phase (ionization enthalpy and electron gain enthalpy) but also on the enthalpy of lattice formation.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
For \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), the ionization enthalpy for \(\mathrm{Na(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na^{+}(g)} + e^{-}\) is \(+495.8\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\), and the electron gain enthalpy for \(\mathrm{Cl(g)} + e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl^{-}(g)}\) is \(-348.7\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). Their sum is \(+147.1\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) (positive), yet solid \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) is highly stable. Thus, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
The enthalpy of lattice formation of \(\mathrm{NaCl(s)}\) from gaseous \(\mathrm{Na^{+}(g)}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}(g)}\) is \(-788\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). This large energy release more than compensates for the \(+147.1\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) absorbed in forming the gaseous ions, resulting in net energy release. Thus, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The stability of ionic solids like \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) is governed by the large negative enthalpy of lattice formation offsetting the positive sum of ionization and electron gain enthalpies. Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_AR_Q09 - Nature of double bond in dicarbon molecule

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): The double bond in the \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\) molecule consists of two \(\pi\) bonds.

Reason (R): In the molecular orbital configuration of \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\), the four electrons after filling \(\sigma 2s\) and \(\sigma^{*} 2s\) occupy the \(\pi 2p_{x}\) and \(\pi 2p_{y}\) molecular orbitals, which are lower in energy than \(\sigma 2p_{z}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In molecular orbital theory, the nature of the bond between two atoms depends on which bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals are occupied by the valence electrons.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
The \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\) molecule has \(12\) electrons, giving a bond order of \(\frac{1}{2}(8 - 4) = 2\), which corresponds to a double bond. Unlike most molecules where a double bond comprises one \(\sigma\) bond and one \(\pi\) bond, the double bond in \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\) consists of two \(\pi\) bonds. Thus, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
For \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\), the molecular orbital energy order places \(\pi 2p_{x} = \pi 2p_{y}\) below \(\sigma 2p_{z}\). Therefore, its electronic configuration is \((\sigma 1s)^{2}(\sigma^{*} 1s)^{2}(\sigma 2s)^{2}(\sigma^{*} 2s)^{2}(\pi 2p_{x}^{2} = \pi 2p_{y}^{2})\). The \(\sigma 2s\) and \(\sigma^{*} 2s\) contributions cancel each other, leaving four electrons in the two \(\pi\) bonding molecular orbitals. Thus, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Because the four net bonding electrons in \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\) reside entirely in the \(\pi 2p_{x}\) and \(\pi 2p_{y}\) orbitals, the double bond consists of both \(\pi\) bonds. Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_AR_Q10 - Lone pair position in sulphur tetrafluoride geometry

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): In \(\mathrm{SF}_{4}\), the lone pair on the central sulphur atom occupies an equatorial position rather than an axial position, giving a see-saw shape.

Reason (R): Placing the lone pair in an equatorial position results in three lone pair–bond pair repulsions at \(90^{\circ}\), whereas placing it in an axial position results in only two lone pair–bond pair repulsions at \(90^{\circ}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a trigonal bipyramidal electron-pair arrangement (\(\mathrm{AB}_{4}\mathrm{E}\) type), the lone pair occupies the position that minimizes \(90^{\circ}\) lone pair–bond pair (\(\mathrm{lp-bp}\)) repulsions.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
In \(\mathrm{SF}_{4}\), the sulphur atom has \(4\) bond pairs and \(1\) lone pair. The lone pair occupies an equatorial position, producing a distorted tetrahedral or see-saw molecular geometry. Thus, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
If the lone pair is placed in an axial position, it is at \(90^{\circ}\) to all three equatorial bond pairs, resulting in three \(\mathrm{lp-bp}\) repulsions at \(90^{\circ}\). If the lone pair is placed in an equatorial position, it is at \(90^{\circ}\) only to the two axial bond pairs, resulting in only two \(\mathrm{lp-bp}\) repulsions at \(90^{\circ}\). Since the Reason states the reverse counts, the Reason is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The equatorial position is favoured because it has fewer (two rather than three) \(90^{\circ}\) \(\mathrm{lp-bp}\) repulsions. Therefore, the Assertion is correct and the Reason is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_AR_Q11 - Instability of dihelium and molecular orbital energies

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): The \(\mathrm{He}_{2}\) molecule is unstable and does not exist.

Reason (R): In the linear combination of atomic orbitals, the bonding molecular orbital has lower energy than the combining atomic orbitals, while the antibonding molecular orbital has higher energy.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Molecular orbital theory predicts molecular stability using bond order, \(\frac{1}{2}(N_{b} - N_{a})\), where a positive bond order indicates a stable molecule and a zero or negative bond order indicates an unstable molecule.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Each helium atom has \(2\) electrons in the \(1s\) orbital, so \(\mathrm{He}_{2}\) has \(4\) electrons with configuration \((\sigma 1s)^{2}(\sigma^{*} 1s)^{2}\). Its bond order is \(\frac{1}{2}(2 - 2) = 0\), which means \(\mathrm{He}_{2}\) is unstable and does not exist. Thus, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
When two atomic orbitals combine via linear combination, the resulting bonding molecular orbital is stabilized (lower energy than the parent atomic orbitals) due to constructive interference, and the antibonding molecular orbital is destabilized (higher energy than the parent atomic orbitals) due to destructive interference. Thus, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Although the Reason correctly describes the relative energies of bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals in general, it does not explain why \(\mathrm{He}_{2}\) is unstable; \(\mathrm{He}_{2}\) is unstable specifically because equal numbers of electrons occupy both \(\sigma 1s\) and \(\sigma^{*} 1s\) orbitals, yielding a bond order of zero. Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
